items._excerpt: Millar Western announced indefinite curtailment of Quesnel River Pulp. Millar Western Forest Products Ltd. will indefinitely curtail operations at its Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertainty surrounding economic fibre supply. The *Quesnel Cariboo Observer* obtained a copy of a letter sent out on Nov. 9, to employees at the Quesnel River Pulp mill. In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. Meyers said the company reviewed all alternatives before concluding that an indefinite curtailment was the only viable option at this time. According to the letter, the duration of the curtailment remains unknown and will depend on market conditions and the availability of economic fibre supply. “As a result, we will be terminating employment for all those impacted and providing severance compensation and other support,” Meyers wrote. He added the company will also provide continuation of certain benefits and access to employee and family assistance resources, with details to be outlined in individual severance letters. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] Nuxalk Nation keeps support services available after fatal grizzly attack
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Nuxalk Nation leaders say the grizzly attack that killed Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, near Bella Coola has renewed trauma in a community still recovering from a separate bear attack last year. The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said forensic evidence linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths. The bears were killed, and investigators believe the attack likely involved rare predatory behaviour. Elected Chief Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner said community support services would remain available for as long as needed. The Nuxalk Nation thanked conservation officers for resolving the incident, while saying the deaths had reopened trauma from the previous attack. Authorities also confirmed the four bears were not involved in that earlier attack, which injured 11 people.

items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, ends Banff rescue-dog program
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [thestar.com] McGill report finds deepfake network spreading false Canada-U.S. trade claims
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

🏔️ ✏️

Holger Peters, a farmer in Schleswig-Holstein, plans to replace grain production on his 340 hectares of arable land with perennial silphium over the next two years. He has planted 125 hectares so far. He says grain production has become barely profitable, while silphium can supply his biogas plant and may also provide a peat substitute for horticultural growing media. Polish cabbage and potato growers are also reporting weak returns: cabbage for processing is selling at about 50 groszy per kilogram, while wholesale potato prices in Łódź ranged from 53 groszy to 1.07 zlotys per kilogram on Oct. 30. Potato farmers have sought higher fuel-tax refunds, but the agriculture ministry has instead pointed to promotional campaigns with retailers.

items.title: [japantoday.com] Serbia’s student-backed list projected to win majority as Vučić concedes defeat
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The student-backed Student List is projected to win a majority in Serbia’s parliament after former President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Sunday’s snap election, ending his Serbian Progressive Party’s 14-year dominance. Vučić said the list could take 135 to 140 of the 250 seats, against about 105 for his party; separate pollster projections put the Student List at 138 seats. The count remained preliminary. Turnout reached 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since Yugoslavia’s breakup in 1992. The election followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway-station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and failures of oversight, accusations the government rejected. The movement’s anti-corruption campaign drew support beyond students, and it entered the election with a slate of civil society candidates. With final results still pending, the Student List faces the task of forming a government without a single established leader. Its candidates have limited political experience. European Union officials offered help with rule-of-law and media reforms, while Vučić alleged foreign interference without providing evidence.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [dailymaverick.co.za] Government agencies take websites offline over PHP remote-code risk
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Government agencies in New York’s Broome County, Idaho and South Africa took websites offline or replaced them with simplified versions on Friday in response to warnings about critical flaws in PHP, the programming language used by nearly 70% of websites whose programming language can be identified. The FBI said the vulnerabilities could let attackers remotely run code in PHP and potentially compromise data and networks. The PHP Foundation released patches and instructions on Wednesday, and the FBI urged organizations to update affected systems or take them offline until they can be secured. Idaho officials said they were prioritizing internet-facing systems and sites supporting public safety and essential government services; Broome County and South Africa’s Presidency had not said in their statements when their websites would be restored. Broome County directed residents seeking county services to call 607-778-8000.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] WMO says powerful El Niño likely to persist through February 2027
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says the strong El Niño developing in the tropical Pacific is expected to peak in December and is nearly certain to persist until February 2027. The climate pattern, which warms the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is forecast to bring above-average temperatures across much of the world and shift rainfall patterns, increasing drought and flood risks in different regions. In Ecuador, the Navy’s Oceanographic and Antarctic Institute reported sea temperatures as much as 5.2°C above normal off Ecuador and Peru. It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [apnews.com] Paraguay president submits resignation as Ueno collapse freezes millions of accounts
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña submitted his resignation on Nov. 5 as the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank froze access to accounts held by nearly 3 million customers. Minutes later, the Chamber of Deputies voted 78-0 to impeach him. Congress had not accepted the resignation by Friday, Nov. 6, leaving Peña formally in office. He said he would appear at the Senate proceedings to defend himself. Vice President Pedro Alliana is next in line if lawmakers accept Peña’s resignation or remove him through impeachment. Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno on Nov. 3 after finding that its solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum. The intervention shut down the bank’s app, cards and transfers. Ueno had about 3 million customers and administered roughly $850 million in public funds, including pension-related money. Lawmakers accuse Peña of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and shielding the bank from scrutiny. He has denied wrongdoing and said the matter should be handled through the courts. Prosecutors ordered three investigations into the bank’s failure, covering oversight, the handling of its collapse and the placement of public funds.

items.title: [latimes.com] El Niño-linked floods force Southwest evacuations; Arizona declares emergency
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pacific storm systems brought torrential rain and flooding across the normally arid Southwest, prompting evacuations in Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. The National Weather Service said El Niño was disrupting weather patterns as the region faced another round of heavy rain. Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declared a statewide emergency Monday to help local authorities clear roads, repair infrastructure and assist displaced residents. At least one person died in the flooding; police said a second death in Flagstaff appeared weather-related, pending an official determination. Former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue estimated that more than 20 trillion gallons of water fell across the Four Corners states and Nevada over two weeks. Flooding damaged roads and bridges, stranded residents and caused sewage to back up into some homes. Although rain had ended in parts of the Southwest by Monday, flooding along some swollen waterways could continue through at least Tuesday.

U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, while professional and business services — a broad category that includes legal, consulting and scientific services — added 70,000 positions. The sector’s gain far exceeded its monthly average of 15,000 over the previous year, but economists said one month of data cannot establish whether artificial intelligence is reducing or creating jobs. Economists quoted by Business Insider said AI is changing the skills employers seek, increasing demand for AI knowledge and critical thinking. The report does not isolate AI’s effects from other influences on employment. Indeed senior economist Cory Stahle said the sector remained below its long-term trend and cautioned against drawing conclusions from a single report. Temporary-help services added 18,600 jobs in October after losing 5,600 in September.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [jns.org] Trump announces plan to end $3.8 billion in annual U.S. aid to Israel
items.content_html:

President Donald Trump said the United States would end its $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, saying he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to the move months earlier. Trump made the announcement on Nov. 3, as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Israel's current 10-year aid agreement runs through 2028, and officials sought clarity on how an early end would work. Vice President JD Vance cited the Iran war and the U.S. relationship with Israel among factors behind Republicans' midterm losses. The incoming Democratic majority takes office in January 2027 and could scrutinize funding for military operations and assistance, though the outgoing Congress could still act on defense legislation before then. Israel's Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a clear majority. President Isaac Herzog said 67 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset recommended opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government, compared with 46 backing Netanyahu. Herzog said he planned to give a lawmaker the mandate on Sunday, Nov. 8, after further talks.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.
